message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code and related laws. Below is an overview of key rights you typically enjoy as a renter: | Category | Typical Tenant Rights (Texas) | Notes | |----------|------------------------------|-------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for residential units; two months for furnished units.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | Landlords must itemize any deductions and provide receipts if requested. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain premises in a safe, sanitary condition.
• Must repair major structural issues, plumbing, heating, electrical, etc., within a reasonable time. | If landlord fails to repair, tenants may withhold rent, repair & deduct, or terminate the lease. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice (except emergencies).
• Notice required: 24 hours for non-emergency entries. | Exceptions include emergencies, inspections, repairs, or showing unit to prospective renters. | | **Lease Terms** | • Written lease is not mandatory but strongly recommended.
• Oral agreements are enforceable but harder to prove. | Lease must specify rent amount, due dates, security deposit, length of tenancy, and any rules. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, except for certain “rent control” areas (none statewide).
• For month‑to‑month leases, landlord must give at least 30 days’ written notice before raising rent. | Some cities have local ordinances limiting increases during COVID‑19 or other circumstances. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for termination of month‑to‑month).
• Eviction requires filing a lawsuit and obtaining a court order. | Tenants can contest eviction in court; they may also negotiate a settlement or move out voluntarily. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Protected classes: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, source of income, etc.
• Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in housing. | Discrimination includes refusing to rent, setting different terms, or evicting based on protected class. | | **Repair & Deduct / Withhold Rent** | • If landlord fails to fix major problems, tenant may pay for repairs and deduct cost from rent, or withhold rent until repaired. | Must follow proper procedure: notify landlord, keep records, and may need to file a claim in small claims court. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must respect privacy; cannot conduct surveillance without consent. | Some states allow landlords to install cameras in common areas, but not inside private rooms. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities unless otherwise specified.
• Tenants may be responsible for water, gas, electricity, trash removal, etc., depending on lease. | Lease should clearly state who pays what. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Tenants may sublet or assign lease only with landlord’s written permission. | Landlord cannot unreasonably deny permission. | | **Maintenance Responsibilities** | • Tenants must keep unit clean, dispose of garbage properly, and avoid damage. | Failure to do so can lead to deductions from security deposit. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand all clauses, especially those about rent, maintenance, and entry. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of notices, emails, text messages, photos of conditions, and receipts for repairs. 3. **Communicate in Writing** – Whenever possible, send notices via email or certified mail to create a paper trail. 4. **Know Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protection laws, such as rent increase caps or eviction moratoriums. 5. **Seek Legal Aid** – If you face eviction or disputes, consult a local attorney or tenant advocacy group. --- #### Quick Reference: When Landlord Can Enter | Situation | Required Notice | Exception | |-----------|-----------------|-----------| | Routine inspection | 24‑hour written notice | None | | Repairs | 24‑hour written notice | Emergencies (e.g., fire, flooding) | | Showing unit to prospective renters | 24‑hour written notice | None | | Emergency (fire, flood, etc.) | Immediate | None | If your landlord enters without proper notice, you may have grounds to sue for trespassing or breach of contract. --- #### Common Issues & Remedies | Issue | Remedy | |-------|--------| | Landlord refuses to return security deposit | File a claim in small claims court (up to $10,000). | | Landlord raises rent without notice | Challenge the increase in court; may be voided. | | Landlord fails to repair a major issue | Repair yourself, deduct cost, or withhold rent; may also file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General. | | Landlord threatens eviction without proper notice | File a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA). | --- ### Resources - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division**: [https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov) - **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs**: [https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us](https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us) - **Local Tenant Advocacy Groups**: e.g., Austin Tenants Union, Dallas Housing Coalition. Feel free to ask if you’d like more detail on any particular aspect—such as how to handle a specific dispute or how to draft a notice letter.
